doc.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

chapter: Learning and views on jazz history
title: Forgotten pre-bebop musicians and Benny Carter
summary: Ingham argues jazz history is taught with a bebop and racial bias, praising Benny Carter, his 1935 BBC work, and swept-aside players like Red Allen and Roy Eldridge.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well it also has a political thing and it has a racial bias too, to be honest, let’s face it. They think jazz is black primarily, well I’m not going to argue that I think that the greatest practitioners have been black musicians — no doubt or question about it — but before that, there were also people playing together. And you know, whites and that. Sadly whites had a monopoly on the radio and the recordings and that kind of stuff. There certainly was a racial barrier there. But blacks were recording very much so. Look at all those blues records that were produced in the 20s. I mean so they weren’t denied their opportunities. But what I’m saying is that a lot of great black musicians from the 30s, people like Henry “Red” Allen, J.C. Higginbotham, Coleman Hawkins even, I mean they’ve been swept under the carpet, but they’ve pretty much been forgotten. People like Frankie Newton, Pete Brown, great innovative players, Chu Berry, Roy Eldridge, Buck Clayton, wonderful trumpet players, who could play rings around Wynton Marsalis. Completely swept under the carpet. I mean they’ve become forgotten people, simply because these instructors think that bebop is the beginning, the fountainhead of it all. So unless you were a part of that bop thing, you were small potatoes.

Well I don’t know, I mean a musician like Benny Carter, who wonderfully is still alive, there is a consummate genius, I mean not only is he a multi-instrumentalist, great arranger, I remember reading the fact that the BBC in their wisdom back in 1935, they hired Benny Carter to come over and they just formed a kind of BBC dance orchestra, and Benny Carter was asked to come over there and arranged for it. And I talked to some of the old time guys who are still alive who played in that band. They said Benny could play every instrument better than anybody in the band, except maybe the piano or something. But he was a terrific trumpet player, he could play all the reeds, and I think he played a little guitar — an extraordinary talent. No, I mean everything starts, and I’m not detracting from Charlie Parker’s genius or anything, but there was a musician of Carter’s statute to me is far more, it transcends Charlie Parker, great as he was. But this was all going on ten, fifteen years ahead of Charlie Parker. And Parker comes out of that. Parker grew out of Jay McShann, and he’d heard all that stuff, he liked, I believe he was quoted as saying he loved Jimmy Dorsey’s alto saxophone playing because it was so technically brilliant. And Parker was a brilliant technician. But you’ve just got to acknowledge the fact that there was life before bebop.

Well it’s interesting too because those people before Parker, a lot of them, they reached a larger audience than Parker ever did. And it’s funny it’s not acknowledged, that bebop is technically demanding, and as wonderful as it was, did not have the audience that some of those before had. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
